14 An unknown mass and a 1.00 kg mass are fixed at opposite ends of a bar. The bar has negligible
mass and a length of 30.0 cm.
The bar balances when supported by a pivot placed 20.0 cm from the unknown mass, as shown.
30.0 cm
unknown mass
1.00 kg mass
bar
20.0 cm
pivot
What is the unknown mass?
A
333 g
B
500 g
C
667 g
D
1000 g

hints: Notice the pivot is $20.0 \text{ cm}$ from the unknown mass on a $30.0 \text{ cm}$ bar, so work out the distance of the $1.00 \text{ kg}$ mass from the pivot.
Recall that for balance the anticlockwise moment about the pivot must equal the clockwise moment, with moment $= \text{force} \times$ perpendicular distance.
Set $m \times 20.0 \text{ cm} = 1.00 \text{ kg} \times 10.0 \text{ cm}$ and solve for $m$, then convert to grams.
walkthrough: Find each perpendicular distance from the pivot. Unknown mass distance $= 20.0 \text{ cm}$. $1.00 \text{ kg}$ mass distance $= 30.0 - 20.0 = 10.0 \text{ cm}$.
Use the principle of moments for equilibrium: sum of clockwise moments $=$ sum of anticlockwise moments about the pivot.
Write weights as $mg$. Let unknown mass be $m$: $m g \times 20.0 \text{ cm} = 1.00 \text{ kg} \times g \times 10.0 \text{ cm}$.
Convert to grams: $0.500 \text{ kg} = 500 \text{ g}$. This is option B.

A.explanation: This would result from using $20.0 \text{ cm}$ for both sides or inverting the ratio incorrectly, not the correct $10.0 \text{ cm}$ and $20.0 \text{ cm}$ distances.

B.explanation: Clockwise moment equals anticlockwise moment with $m \times 20.0 = 1.00 \times 10.0$, giving $m = 0.500 \text{ kg} = 500 \text{ g}$.

C.explanation: This confuses mass and weight ratio and uses $20.0/30.0$ instead of $10.0/20.0$ for the balance of moments about the pivot.

D.explanation: This assumes equal masses balance at any pivot position, ignoring that the pivot is $20.0 \text{ cm}$ from one end and only $10.0 \text{ cm}$ from the other.
